title: Live: More people will take up smoking if tobacco excise is reduced, minister says
description: Clare O'Neil says reducing the tobacco excise to address the rising take-up of illicit tobacco will not help Australians give up smoking. Follow live.
content_snippet: Australia will seek to harness the benefits of artificial intelligence without losing control of it by tackling challenges such as data centres, copyright, and jobs through a new national framework. …
author: Joshua Boscaini
full_text: Federal politics: Labor to force data centres to minimise water, underwrite own power under new AI standards — as it happened New artificial intelligence data centres will be forced to underwrite or supply their own power and minimise their use of water under new AI standards to be introduced to parliament. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has also announced the creation of an Office of AI within his department to oversee the design of the new AI standards. Look back on the developments on our live blog. Submit a comment or question Live updates New: Filters Choose what information you see below by using filters Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 2:26pm Greenpeace joins call for pause on AI data centres The government's approach will be considered by the national cabinet in August, with standards expected to be legislated early next year. Greenpeace Australia Pacific has released a statement joining the Greens' call for a pause on all AI data centre development until those new rules are in place. Joe Rafalowicz from Greenpeace says the government is "kicking the can down the road". "Australians right around the country are calling for urgent regulations on AI data centres that are already being built in their backyard," he says. "We urgently need a moratorium on AI data centre approvals until there are binding rules in place to protect our communities, our climate and our environment." Key Event Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 2:17pm Unions welcome AI 'intervention' There's been a lot reported about what the union movement wants from the government on AI regulation, and next weekend at the National Labor Conference it's expected to be a contested topic. It is the job of the unions to advocate for the rights of workers, including those at risk of losing their jobs to AI. The Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) has released a statement responding to Anthony Albanese's AI speech, and it seems relatively happy. "It’s good the government is taking a more active role in AI policy, and is willing to take action to ensure that it benefits Australians," ACTU boss Sally McManus says. “We welcome the PM’s strong stance against the theft of creative works and the government's consistent refusal to give big tech an exemption from having to pay for the copyrighted content they use." McManus insists the unions don't want to veto the use of technology, but "only to veto the harm it could cause". “Australians don't trust AI because of the lack of clear benefit for working people. We have had big promises, but so far, no guarantee that any benefits will be shared with workers," she says. Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 2:08pm Government's AI approach 'still lagging' says Chaney Independent Kate Chaney says she's worried the government's focus appears largely directed toward physical infrastructure. “While data centre standards are important, there are many broader known and emerging risks the government is still failing to prioritise," she says. Among the issues outlined in a discussion paper on AI that Chaney released last month are questions about the taxation of AI companies, and the prevalence of AI deepfakes and misinformation. "Tech companies are very good at minimising their Australian tax by re-routing profits to low-tax havens overseas," Chaney says. "We need to ensure we have an effective mechanism to keep some of the economic value in Australia." Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 1:51pm Greens call for pause on data centres until mandatory standards are in place The Greens say the government should impose an indefinite pause on any data centre developments until mandatory regulatory rules are in effect. Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young has called AI "the new extractive industry" and says without the right regulation, big tech companies will take Australia's resources "and leave Australians with nothing to show for it". "It is essential that we get the rules right. To do that, we need a pause on the approval and construction of new hyperscale data centres while we do this important policy work," she says. "Just because big tech companies want to move at hyperspeed, doesn't mean that we need to fast-track and roll out the red carpet for them." Key Event Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 1:30pm Climate Council says Labor must tie new data centres to new renewable energy The Climate Council says the government's new Office for AI must tie the development of new data centres to additional renewable energy. The council has welcomed the prime minister's announcements, and says the way the standards are implemented will determine whether Australians are protected against power price hikes. Climate Council chief executive Amanda McKenzie says the government must regulate data centre growth to ensure it occurs in Australia's best interests. "The AI-driven surge in data centres will have a profound effect on our energy system, and unchecked, this growth could mean soaring prices and rampant climate pollution," McKenzie says. "Australia is a very attractive location for data centre proponents, but it means that we need strong guardrails to protect our standard of living. We need these things to work for us. "This means upholding Prime Minister [Anthony] Albanese's pledge today that data centres match their energy demand with new renewables and storage to shield households and other businesses from increased costs." Key Event Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 1:10pm Greens say PM's AI speech 'missed the moment', won't protect Australians Greens senator David Shoebridge is up to provide his immediate reaction to the prime minister's speech on artificial intelligence. Shoebridge says the PM's speech "missed the moment" and that the new Office of AI won't provide the AI protections people want. The NSW Greens senator says the office will be a "door that the big tech industry can knock on to get what they want". He says the parliament needs to legislate clear protections to protect Australia's creative industries, jobs and environment. "Instead, what we got today from the prime minister was basically an invitation to us, big tech, to come up and establish themselves in this country with even more rapid approvals," Albanese says. Shoebridge has called for a moratorium on new data centres until legislated protections are in place. Key Event Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 12:53pm Here are the main takeaways from the PM's AI speech Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has just concluded his speech on the government's approach to artificial intelligence. Here are the key takeaways and announcements from his speech to the University of Sydney: - The prime minister has announced the federal government will legislate national standards for artificial intelligence. - The standards, which the PM hopes will pass parliament early next year, will create a "legal obligation" for the next generation of data centres. - Under the standards, data centres will be forced to minimise water usage and underwrite or supply their own power. - AI companies will be barred from using Australian books, music, art or news to build or train AI without the consent and control of the creators. - Premiers and chief ministers will be consulted on the standards at the national cabinet meeting next month, according to the PM. - Albanese has also confirmed the creation of an Office of AI within the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet. - The office will coordinate the design of Australia's new national AI standards and bring together work across government. Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 12:38pm Albanese says Australians shouldn't view AI as a threat to good jobs In conclusion, the prime minister says Australia shouldn't treat artificial intelligence as a threat to jobs. Anthony Albanese says we must use AI as an instrument to help create good jobs in Australia. He says he's confident that Australia can make the technology work in the national interest. "If we move with purpose now, if we back ourselves, if we trust in our values and invest in our people, if we set our national standards high, then I have every confidence that Australia can seize this moment and make it our own," Albanese says. Key Event Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 12:35pm PM confirms Office of AI within his department And, as expected, the prime minister has announced that, from today, a new Office of AI will be established in his department. Anthony Albanese says the office will work with the industry and innovation minister, and science and technology assistant minister. He says the new office will liaise with all ministers and departments to deal with opportunities and concerns arising from AI. The PM says it will coordinate the design of Australia's new national standards and bring together the work ministers across government are working on. Key Event Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 12:31pm Date centres to underwrite power, minimise water use under new AI standards: PM Anthony Albanese is providing some details as to what the national artificial intelligence standards legislation will look like. The prime minister says it will spell out "plain as day" that artists' creative endeavour is their work and property, He says it will outline that no companies should use Australian books, music, art or news to build or train AI without the creator's control. "No country has got this right yet. Nowhere do artists or rights holders have sufficient control of their work when it comes to AI training," Albanese says. "And that is why the best way to secure the strongest copyright protections for Australian artists is for Australia to be active and involved." Albanese says the standards will set clear rules for the next generation of "large data centres". Those rules will detail where the data centres can be built and explain how much power and water they will be able use. The PM says the government will ensure data centre companies and centres underwrite new power supplies, and limit how much water they can use. "We'll create a legal obligation for the next generation of large-scale data centres to underwrite new power supply, to pay their full share of grid connection, so no costs are passed on to homes or businesses," he says. Key Event Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 12:26pm PM announces govt will legislate standards for artificial intelligence next year Anthony Albanese says the government will establish a set of standards for artificial intelligence. He says he will seek agreement from state premiers and territory chief ministers at a national cabinet meeting next month. The government, he says, will aim to bring legislation before parliament and carry it early next year. "It is not our goal to try and legislate for every possible eventuality or risk. That only creates risk of Australia missing out on investment altogether," Albanese says. "This is about having the flexibility to keep pace with change and get out in front of it so Australia can draw on and learn from what other countries are doing, and deal with issues in real time, without the bureaucracy." Key Event Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 12:23pm Albanese says standing still on AI risks Australian workers, sovereignty The prime minister says Australia is an attractive destination for artificial intelligence companies because it is a stable democracy. He says Australia is at the top of the global ladder for integrity, security of transactions and timeliness of payments. Anthony Albanese says Australia must be ambitious about the opportunities presented by artificial intelligence. He says if Australia stands still, the opportunities presented by AI will "run right on the top of us". "If we descend into self-doubt or wander out into the global market as a disparate collection of states and councils and companies and firms, rather than as one country, then others will write the rules and maybe they will play by them," Albanese says. "That would not only risk the integrity of Australian artists and journalists, it would mean subcontracting our national sovereignty and security to the control of foreign monopolies, and relegating our workers and our economy to the last link of the digital supply chain." Key Event Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 12:19pm PM says govt can't turn its back on AI, must make technology work in Australia's interests Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is moving onto artificial intelligence now and he says the government can't turn its back on AI. He says not embracing AI would effectively mean cutting Australians off from opportunities. He says Australia has to set the terms of AI's social licence, but that it has to be done now and not left any longer. Albanese says the government wants to attract AI investment and support and create new AI jobs. "The fact that we cannot stop change does not render us powerless," Albanese says. "If we act now, if we mobilise our resources and coordinate our efforts, if we move with the urgency that the speed of this change demands, if we build to match the scale of the opportunity that this moment presents, and if we do it the Australian way, true to our values and our standards, we can make AI work in Australia's national interests." Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 12:14pm Albanese begins AI speech with examples of Australian reforms The PM has just stepped up to the podium and he's started by talking about Australian reforms, such as Medicare and eight-hour work days. He's also pointed to the federal government's social media ban for under-16s, which he said sent a signal and "set a standard". Anthony Albanese says the social media ban is an example of Australia applying its "enduring values" to policy. "It is proof of what Australia can do when we back ourselves, where we apply our enduring values to the challenges that are presented by new technologies," Albanese says. "We can set a standard that changes the way the world looks at an issue and deals with it." He says Australians are eager adopters of new technology and that's the choice that Australia has for artificial intelligence. Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 12:01pm PM set to deliver speech on national AI framework Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will soon step up to deliver a speech mapping out a national framework for artificial intelligence. We expect the PM to announce a new Office of AI in his department to oversee and coordinate the design of AI standards. Albanese isn't expected to announce any dramatic shift in the federal government's position on copyright law for creatives. If you want to catch up on what the PM will be talking about, read the story below by my colleague Clare Armstrong. Otherwise, stick around and we'll bring you the prime minister's speech as it happens here on the federal politics blog. Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 11:57am Dan Tehan says GenCost report shows Labor's net zero targets are causing 'energy havoc' Shadow Energy Minister Dan Tehan has weighed into the CSIRO's annual GenCost released today. The report, completed by Australia's peak science agency, found batteries are now cheaper at supplying peak demand for power than gas. It notes insatiable demand for gas-fired power from US data centres is driving up turbine costs. In a statement, Tehan says the report shows the government's net zero will drive an increase in energy costs. "The GenCost report confirms that Labor's all-or-nothing net zero obsession will lead to higher power bills for Australian families," Tehan says. "Labor's focus on hitting mandatory climate targets is causing energy havoc when their focus should be on delivering the cheapest, most reliable forms of energy." Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 11:36am Analysis: What would Australia's economy look like under One Nation? If One Nation forms government what would Australia's economy look like? Pauline Hanson's speech at the National Press Club on June 17 detailed large parts of her economic vision. In recent days, One Nation's treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce has talked about the Reserve Bank and how he thinks it should behave. And Hanson has said that she takes policy advice from Gina Rinehart, the mining billionaire she considers a friend. Read the full analysis from business reporter Gareth Hutchens in the link below. Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 10:31am Batteries 'cheaper' than gas plants as data centres fuel turbine costs Runaway demand for turbines from data centres in the US is for the first time making new gas-fired power uncompetitive with batteries in the evening electricity consumption peak, a report has found. Australia's top science agency, the CSIRO, said batteries were helping lower high evening power prices as the technology's costs fell and significant extra capacity was added. At the same time, the CSIRO said, the costs of gas-fired power were rising as insatiable demand from data centres caused a shortage of the giant turbines at the heart of gas plants. Read the full story from energy reporter Daniel Mercer and climate editor Tim Leslie in the link below. Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 10:03am Taylor categorically rules out coalition with One Nation Opposition leader Angus Taylor says he will not enter into a Coalition with Pauline Hanson's One Nation party. "I'm ruling it out," Taylor told 7.30 last night. "There is no plan to form any kind of coalition with One Nation." Taylor was adamant that the current Coalition with the National Party would not be changing as he again attacked One Nation's policies, as he did last week. He said its policies would lead the nation to economic ruin. "One Nation would, as a government, leave us with an eternity of pain," he said. Key Event Wed 15 Jul 2026 at 9:39am Angus Taylor says he hasn't seen post by Liberal senator on Indian migration The Australian reports Liberal frontbencher Jacinta Nampijinpa Price shared a right-wing post that claims the government is importing migrants from India, Africa and the Middle East for electoral gain. The post was from the 2 Worlds Collide Podcast reacting to a segment on Insiders on Sunday. But Opposition leader Angus Taylor says he hasn't seen the post that Nampijinpa Price shared on X, formerly Twitter. "I haven't seen it, so it's very hard to comment on it," Taylor says. But pressed later on whether he would counsel his team against reposting such content, Taylor says the right level of skilled migration has served Australia well. "That model of immigration has been enormously successful [and] is the Australian multiculturalism that I believe in, that's distinctive, enormously successful and it's been good for our country," he said. Pressed again on the Liberal senator's shared post, Taylor says "the best disinfectant for any disinformation is people saying that that's wrong".
